title: OpenTelemetry Trace Bottleneck Analysis in Microservice Mesh
businessContext: A ride-hailing and delivery dispatch API has a P99 latency SLA of 500ms. In production, P99 latency has drifted to 4,200ms. Because the request passes through API Gateway, Order Service, Driver Matching Service, Pricing Service, and Notification Service, engineers are blaming each other's services.
problemStatement: Analyze the OpenTelemetry distributed trace waterfall JSON. Trace spans reveal that Driver Matching Service calls Pricing Service sequentially in a loop for 20 candidate drivers instead of a single batch call. Refactor the service interaction to use parallel / batch gRPC calls and identify how trace context propagation (`traceparent` header) tracks requests across boundaries.
constraints: P99 request latency must drop below 400ms.
Must preserve W3C TraceContext propagation across HTTP / gRPC calls.
Transform N sequential remote calls into a single batch call or parallel execution with bounded concurrency.
candidateTasks: Inspect span waterfall: identify parent span, child spans, and sequential time gap.
Refactor sequential calls to batch RPC `pricingClient.getBatchDriverQuotes(...)` or bounded `Promise.all()`.
Explain the format of the W3C `traceparent` header: `00-trace_id-parent_id-trace_flags`.
hints: In a distributed trace waterfall, sequential calls show up as a staircase pattern where each bar starts only after the previous bar finishes.
Batching remote calls into a single payload reduces network round-trip serialization overhead to a single hop.

testCases.name: Eliminates sequential RPC waterfall and batches remote calls

alternativeApproaches: Parallel calls via `Promise.all` with a concurrency limiter (`p-limit(5)`) if the downstream service does not yet support batching.
commonMistakes: Firing 100 concurrent un-throttled calls with Promise.all, which overwhelms the downstream service connection pool and causes connection timeouts.
Failing to propagate trace context headers, which causes downstream spans to show up as orphaned root traces in Datadog/Jaeger.
